The [[global-star-formation-suppression-mechanism|regulation of star formation]] and the cosmic baryon cycle is fundamentally governed by the interplay between a galaxy's interstellar medium and its vast surrounding reservoir, the circumgalactic medium (CGM). Without regulatory mechanisms, cosmological gas accretion would lead to a catastrophic [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]], producing galaxies with unphysically high stellar masses [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.417..950H/abstract). To prevent this, galaxies rely on [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]] driven by [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] and [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]]. The macroscopic efficiency of these feedback processes is canonically parameterized by two dimensionless quantities: the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] ($\eta_M$) and the [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy-loading factor]] ($\eta_E$). The mass-loading factor measures the ratio of the gas mass ejection rate to the galaxy's star formation rate, quantifying the strength of direct ejective feedback. Conversely, the energy-loading factor compares the kinetic and thermal energy outflow rate to the total theoretical energy budget supplied by stellar or black hole sources, quantifying the capacity for [[negative-feedback|preventative heating]] within the extended halo [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). 

Historically, theoretical models heavily relied on massive ejective outflows—characterized by $\eta_M \gg 1$—to physically expel gas and suppress star formation, particularly in low-mass dwarf galaxies. However, modern paradigms increasingly emphasize the role of preventative feedback, where the energy-loading factor plays the pivotal role in heating the CGM to offset radiative cooling and stifle further gas accretion [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [Tumlinson et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ARA&A..55..389T/abstract). Through a combination of early [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]], mechanical supernova feedback, and energetic AGN jets, the CGM is maintained in a marginally precipitating state, self-regulating near a critical ratio of cooling time to freefall time. Counterintuitively, recent analytical frameworks suggest that strictly increasing mass ejection can sometimes elevate [[equilibrium-star-formation-rates|Equilibrium star formation rates]]; if too much mass is loaded into the lower halo, the galaxy must form more stars to generate the necessary supernova energy to resist the gravitational contraction of its atmospheric gas. Furthermore, it is now understood that [[stellar-and-agn-feedback|Stellar and AGN Feedback]] are not strictly independent but non-linearly couple to regulate the structural and [[galaxy-chemical-enrichment-mechanisms|chemical evolution]] of the halo.

This article explores the fundamental physics and observational signatures of mass and energy loading within the galactic ecosystem. It tracks the historical development of feedback models, details the distinct physical drivers of ejective and preventative feedback across different halo mass regimes, and examines the [[self-regulated-feedback-mechanisms|Self-regulated feedback mechanisms]] governing the multiphase CGM. Additionally, the text reviews how current cosmological simulations implement these processes through varied subgrid physics, and how these choices profoundly impact [[galactic-gas-dynamics-and-flows|gas dynamics]] and metal distributions. Finally, it outlines the open questions at the frontier of the field. These include the "missing baryon problem" in Milky Way-mass halos, the tension between simulated and observed O VI absorption column densities, the potential for energetic events to drive [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]] in the high-redshift universe [Ferrara et al. (2004)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2004astro.ph..6554F/abstract), [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract), and how upcoming multi-wavelength observations will ultimately constrain the true mass and energy budgets of the circumgalactic medium.

## Introduction to Mass and Energy Loading Factors

To quantify the efficiency of [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]] in regulating the baryon cycle, models typically parameterize the macroscopic effects of feedback using two fundamental dimensionless parameters: the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] ($\eta_M$) and the [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy-loading factor]] ($\eta_E$). These parameters describe the rates at which mass and energy are injected into the circumgalactic medium (CGM) relative to a galaxy's [[star-formation-processes|star formation rate]] and the theoretical energy budget provided by massive stars.

The mass-loading factor is defined as the ratio of the gas mass outflow rate, $\dot{M}_{\rm wind}$, to the star formation rate (SFR):
$$ \eta_M = \frac{\dot{M}_{\rm wind}}{\text{SFR}} $$
Similarly, the energy-loading factor is the ratio of the energy outflow rate, $\dot{E}_{\rm wind}$, to the available energy injection rate from supernovae, $\dot{E}_{\rm SN}$:
$$ \eta_E = \frac{\dot{E}_{\rm wind}}{\dot{E}_{\rm SN}} $$
Together with the metal-loading factor ($\eta_Z$), these parameters dictate how galaxies avoid the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]]. They do so via two primary channels: physically ejecting gas from the interstellar medium (ejective feedback, governed by $\eta_M$) and heating the CGM to stifle future cosmological accretion ([[negative-feedback|preventative feedback]], governed by $\eta_E$) [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract).

Historically, phenomenological models have relied on heavily mass-loaded winds to reproduce the observed stellar-to-halo mass relations, postulating that large quantities of gas must be expelled to suppress excessive star formation. However, the literature is currently in active debate regarding whether high $\eta_M$ values are strictly necessary. Recent frameworks suggest that self-regulation can be achieved primarily through high energy loading, shifting the paradigm from purely ejective to preventative feedback. For instance, gas-regulator models demonstrate that Milky Way-like halos can successfully match empirical scaling relations using low mass-loading ($\eta_M \sim 0.1-10$) paired with modest energy-loading ($\eta_E \sim 0.1$). Conversely, lower-mass halos require highly efficient energy coupling, approaching $\eta_E \sim 1$ [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). 

Furthermore, the simple ejective suppression paradigm has been challenged by recent thermodynamic models of galactic atmospheres. In some formulations, [[equilibrium-star-formation-rates|Equilibrium star formation rates]] in low-mass galaxies are found to be largely insensitive to $\eta_M$ [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract). Counterintuitively, these models predict that increasing $\eta_M$ can actually result in *more* star formation; the galaxy must form additional stars to provide the necessary supernova energy to resist the gravitational contraction of the surrounding atmospheric gas [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract).

Both modern cosmological simulations and high-redshift observations reveal complex scaling behaviors for these loading factors. In the IllustrisTNG simulations, the mass-loading factor strongly correlates with environment, decreasing with both increasing halo mass and increasing redshift. In contrast, the energy-loading factor remains nearly constant across these varying mass and redshift regimes [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract). Direct observational constraints remain challenging to obtain, but recent high-resolution JWST spectroscopy of sub-$L^\star$ galaxies at $z \sim 4-8$ measures mass-loading factors ranging from $\eta_M = 0.04$ to $0.4$. These outflows frequently exceed local escape velocities, confirming that high-redshift galaxies are highly efficient at removing baryons and enriching the early CGM [Saldana-Lopez et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250117145S/abstract).

## Historical Development and the Overcooling Problem

Early cosmological simulations of galaxy formation revealed a fundamental discrepancy between theoretical predictions and observations of the local universe. In the absence of energetic feedback, radiatively cooling gas in dark matter halos rapidly loses pressure support and collapses into the central regions. This runaway condensation, widely known as the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]], results in global star formation rates that exceed observed values by one to two orders of magnitude [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.417..950H/abstract). Consequently, models lacking feedback severely overpredict the galaxy mass function at both the low- and high-mass extremes, yielding massive galaxies that are unphysically blue and star-forming. Despite these early challenges, historical studies mapping the mass distribution in the Milky Way successfully demonstrated that inner galactic structures are intrinsically dominated by baryons, and that early bulge formation could proceed efficiently from clumpy, gas-rich disks [Gerhard et al. (2006)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2006EAS....20...89G/abstract). Even prior to cosmological frameworks, foundational stability models of the multi-phase ISM successfully reconciled thermal pressures with observations of cold, warm, and hot gas components, including early O VI detections [Cowie et al. (1987)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1987ASSL..134..245C/abstract).

The earliest attempts to solve the overcooling problem focused on injecting thermal energy from supernovae (SNe) directly into the surrounding interstellar medium (ISM). However, simple thermal injection proved highly ineffective. Because SNe typically explode in dense molecular clouds where the radiative cooling time is significantly shorter than the dynamical time, the injected thermal energy radiates away before it can perform macroscopic $P\,dV$ work on the gas. To circumvent this "cooling catastrophe," theorists relied on [[heuristic-models|Heuristic models]]. These early, ad-hoc implementations included temporarily disabling radiative cooling for heated gas particles, artificially reducing the density of the heated gas, or directly imposing kinetic velocity kicks to surrounding fluid elements. While these subgrid treatments successfully suppressed star formation—yielding relations consistent with the expectation that a galaxy's luminosity scales with its specific binding energy as $L \propto M V_c^2 \propto M^{5/3}$, where $V_c$ is the circular velocity—they were fundamentally phenomenological and heavily dependent on numerical resolution. This marked a vital progression from purely analytical studies to explicit numerical models capable of capturing supernova feedback across both superbubble and galactic scales [Hensler et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011IAUS..270..309H/abstract).

The historical development of feedback models eventually shifted away from these numerical workarounds toward physically motivated, [[multi-scale-multi-science-systems|multi-scale]] frameworks. It became clear that robustly solving the overcooling problem required properly coupling the ISM to the vast baryonic reservoir of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) [Tumlinson et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ARA&A..55..389T/abstract). To efficiently unbind or heat gas in low-mass halos, modern treatments of [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] incorporate early, pre-supernova momentum input (such as [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]] and stellar winds). This early feedback disperses dense giant molecular clouds within $\sim 3$ Myr, dramatically lowering the local density before the first SNe detonate, which allows the subsequent mechanical energy to escape the ISM and couple to the CGM with minimal radiative losses [Agertz et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...770...25A/abstract), [Chevance et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract).

In more massive halos ($\gtrsim 10^{12} M_\odot$), however, stellar feedback alone cannot prevent late-time cooling flows. Resolving the high-mass end of the overcooling problem required the integration of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]]. Energy injected by supermassive black holes via relativistic jets and radiation provides the requisite [[non-gravitational-heating|Non-gravitational heating]] to offset radiative losses in the extended halo, maintaining the CGM in an elevated entropy state that stifles further accretion [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract), [Harrison et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023arXiv230703770H/abstract). Today, the prevailing paradigm views galaxy evolution not as a one-way monolithic collapse, but as a self-regulated ecosystem where the precise balance of mass-loading (ejective feedback) and energy-loading (preventative feedback) modulates the thermodynamics of the CGM [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract).

## Stellar Feedback and Ejective Processes in Low-Mass Halos

Low-mass and dwarf galaxies ($M_* < 10^9 M_\odot$) are highly susceptible to stellar feedback owing to their shallow gravitational potential wells [Collins et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022NatAs...6..647C/abstract). The regulation of star formation in these environments relies heavily on a multiphase [[sn-feedback-model|SN feedback model]], which is fundamentally preceded by [[strong-pre-sn-feedback|Strong pre-SN feedback]]. Before the first supernovae detonate, early feedback mechanisms—specifically stellar winds, [[radiative-feedback|photoionization]], and [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]]—inject momentum into the interstellar medium (ISM) [Agertz et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...770...25A/abstract). Observations of nearby star-forming disks indicate that these processes disperse giant molecular clouds within $\sim 3$ Myr of the emergence of [[massive-star-physics|massive stars]] [Chevance et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract). By clearing dense gas, pre-SN feedback mitigates severe radiative cooling losses, allowing subsequent supernova blast waves to propagate efficiently into the circumgalactic medium (CGM) rather than stalling in the ISM [Lucas et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493.4700L/abstract). Furthermore, this early feedback combined with subsequent energetic ejections in faint early-universe galaxies likely facilitated the escape of ionizing radiation, playing a critical role in driving the Epoch of Reionization [Erb et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015Natur.523..169E/abstract). The energy deposition from these early galaxies drove the profound phase transition of the intergalactic medium (IGM) into a warm, ionized state during cosmic reionization [Ferrara et al. (2014)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2014arXiv1409.4946F/abstract). Analyzing this reionization-era phenomenology, including the distribution of UV radiation fields and gas densities, provides essential clues to the formation time of these very first generations of galaxies [Lidz et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ASSL..423...23L/abstract).

The primary metric for ejective feedback efficiency is the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]], defined as the ratio of the gas outflow rate to the star formation rate:
$$ \eta_M = \frac{\dot{M}_{\rm wind}}{\dot{M}_*} $$
Observations of high-redshift ($z=4-7.6$) sub-$L^\star$ galaxies reveal highly efficient baryon removal, with mass-loading factors ranging from $0.04$ to $0.4$ and outflow velocities exceeding the local escape velocity [Saldana-Lopez et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250117145S/abstract). At $z \sim 0$, these ejective processes result in the CGM acting as the dominant baryon reservoir for dwarf galaxies. For example, the CGM of the Local Group dwarf Sextans B contains $\sim 8 \times 10^8 M_\odot$ of cool gas, which is roughly 20 times the mass of its combined stellar and H I disk [Fox et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260100437F/abstract). Across simulated dwarf populations, approximately $48\%$ of all baryons within the virial radius reside in the CGM, predominantly in a warm ($10^{4.5} - 10^{5.5}$ K) phase that retains a significant fraction of the metals formed by the galaxy [Piacitelli et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250508861P/abstract). Moreover, the hot X-ray emitting phase of these superwinds contains the majority of the injected energy and newly-synthesized metals, making it the component most likely to permanently escape the host halo [Strickland et al. (2009)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2009astro2010S.289S/abstract).

While historical subgrid models relied heavily on massive ejective winds (high $\eta_M$) to suppress dwarf galaxy growth, modern frameworks highlight the necessity of combining this mass removal with high energy-loading factors ($\eta_E \sim 1$) to sufficiently heat the CGM and [[negative-feedback|prevent further accretion]] [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). Furthermore, the physical impact of these outflows on the CGM is acutely sensitive to the chosen numerical implementation. Cosmological [[galaxy-chemical-enrichment-mechanisms|chemical evolution]] simulations demonstrate that [[mechanical-feedback|Mechanical feedback]]—which explicitly models the terminal momentum of supernova remnants—reproduces observed [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|Metallicity Distributions and Scaling Relations]] far better than purely thermal or kinetic energy injections [Ibrahim et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.527.3276I/abstract), [Ibrahim et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.544..815I/abstract). However, varying the efficiency of [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] not only alters the ISM structure but also non-linearly affects the timing and efficiency of subsequent AGN feedback in more massive progenitors [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241016361M/abstract), underscoring the complex, [[multi-scale-multi-science-systems|multi-scale]] nature of galactic outflows.

## AGN Feedback and Preventative Heating in Massive Galaxies

In massive halos ($M_{\rm halo} \gtrsim 10^{12} M_\odot$), galaxy self-regulation is primarily driven by preventative feedback from [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]]. While low-mass galaxies rely heavily on ejective stellar feedback characterized by a high [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] ($\eta_M$), massive galaxies operate in a regime where the [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy loading factor]] ($\eta_E$) becomes the dominant regulatory parameter [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). [[negative-feedback|Preventative feedback]] throttles accretion by injecting thermal and kinetic energy into the circumgalactic medium (CGM), raising the entropy of the gas and offsetting radiative cooling without necessarily ejecting large masses of gas from the deep dark matter potential well [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). 

Analyses of cosmological simulations, such as IllustrisTNG, reveal that while mass loading strongly decreases with increasing halo mass and increasing redshift, energy loading remains remarkably constant across these regimes [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract). Phenomenological models reproducing the stellar-to-halo mass relation typically require energy loading factors of $\eta_E \sim 0.1$ for Milky Way-like halos, rising to $\eta_E \sim 1$ for lower-mass systems [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). AGN supply this [[non-gravitational-heating|Non-gravitational heating]] via two primary channels: a "quasar mode" dominated by radiation and wide-angle winds, and a "radio mode" dominated by highly collimated, mechanical jets [Fabian et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ARA&A..50..455F/abstract). The efficiency and directionality of jet feedback are heavily influenced by the black hole spin [Huško et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250905179H/abstract). Even low-power kinetic modes can drastically influence the galaxy; for example, observations of the disk galaxy VV 340a demonstrate that a precessing low-power jet can drive widespread, significant gas outflows that directly impact the host's star formation capabilities [Kader et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108791K/abstract). The efficiency of AGN feedback is also intricately linked to the host galaxy's disk geometry. In systems with thin disks, injected energy can easily escape via polar directions, whereas thick gas disks confine the expanding bubbles, drastically increasing the $P\,dV$ work done on the ISM [Sivasankaran et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240215240S/abstract). Furthermore, the inclusion of X-ray radiation fields can enhance the preventative impact of AGN by heating gas at large radii, suppressing star formation by up to a factor of two compared to purely local, thermal injection models [Hambrick et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011ApJ...738...16H/abstract). To characterize this negative feedback and accurately trace the kinematics of AGN-driven outflows, observations increasingly rely on cold molecular gas, which serves as a vital diagnostic of the mass and energy being evacuated from the host galaxy [Morganti et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017FrASS...4...42M/abstract).

The interaction between [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] and AGN feedback is highly non-linear. Standard theory often assumes these feedback sources are independent or additive, but hydrodynamic simulations demonstrate that supernovae and AGN can mutually weaken each other's effects, particularly in the halo mass range for which both feedback processes are efficient [Booth et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013NatSR...3.1738B/abstract), [Booth et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013NatSR....E1738B/abstract). For instance, strong stellar feedback can lower central gas densities, which delays the onset of rapid black hole growth and shifts the subsequent AGN feedback phase to higher halo masses [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241016361M/abstract). Consequently, both processes must be modeled simultaneously to accurately estimate the total [[mass-quenching-efficiency|Mass quenching efficiency]] of a galaxy.

While AGN energy injection is traditionally viewed as a mechanism for negative feedback, the literature reflects an ongoing debate regarding its capacity to trigger star formation. Under certain conditions, overpressurized AGN outflows can compress cold gas clouds in the ISM and inner CGM, inducing [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]] [Bieri et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...812L..36B/abstract). Similarly, rapid positive feedback on timescales of $<0.15$ Myr has been empirically observed locally as driven by massive stars (stellar feedback) compressing their surrounding environments [Luisi et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021SciA....7.9511L/abstract). This positive feedback regime is hypothesized to have been prevalent in the gas-rich early universe ($z \gtrsim 6$), before galaxies transitioned into the energy-conserving, preventative quenching mode that dominates the local universe [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract).

## The Multiphase CGM as a Baryon and Metal Reservoir

The circumgalactic medium (CGM) is a complex, multi-phase environment that serves as the dominant gas reservoir for both baryons and metals in a dark matter halo. Rather than an inert repository, it is a dynamic ecosystem shaped by the cumulative history of mass and energy loading from [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]]. Observations of fast radio bursts (FRBs) constrain the Milky Way's CGM mass to $< 10^{11} M_\odot$, implying that the total baryonic mass of the halo is $\lesssim 60\%$ of the cosmological average due to efficient feedback ejection [Ravi et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025AJ....169..330R/abstract). At the low-mass extreme, the CGM of dwarf galaxies harbors $\sim 48\%$ of all halo baryons—up to 20 times the combined mass of their stellar and H I disk components [Piacitelli et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250508861P/abstract), [Fox et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260100437F/abstract). There is a direct physical connection between the H I gas fractions within a galaxy's disk and the Ly$\alpha$ equivalent widths measured in its CGM, underscoring that the CGM actively nourishes the interstellar gas supply [Borthakur et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...813...46B/abstract). Recent findings from the DIISC survey reveal that the Ly$\alpha$ equivalent width is actually best predicted by the impact parameter normalized by the galaxy's H I radius, rather than the traditional virial radius [Borthakur et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240912554B/abstract). This spatial connection extends to enriched gas as well; metal ions like Si III and C II are better traced by their distance relative to the H I disk, further underscoring the tight physical coupling between the CGM and the interstellar gas supply [Koplitz et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250202583K/abstract).

The stability of this multi-phase medium is governed by the thermodynamic balance between radiative cooling and preventative heating. Maintaining this phase structure requires significant non-thermal support; single-phase photoionization models fail to simultaneously reproduce the observed low- and high-ionization absorption species. Instead, multi-phase models (such as MAIHEM) incorporating a 3D turbulent velocity dispersion of $\sigma_{\rm 3D} \gtrsim 26$ km s$^{-1}$ are required to successfully match these observations, yielding preferred metallicities of $Z/Z_\odot \approx 40\%$ [Buie et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...890...33B/abstract). Additionally, cosmic ray pressure can profoundly alter gas kinematics, providing buoyancy that produces narrower O VI and broader Si III absorption profiles that better align with observations [Butsky et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...935...69B/abstract).

As the primary sink for ejected material, the CGM is crucial for understanding [[metallicity-distributions-and-scaling-relations|Metallicity Distributions and Scaling Relations]] within the halo, which are highly sensitive to the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] and the balance between [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] and [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]]. The high-ionization O VI $\lambda\lambda 1031, 1037$ doublet serves as a premier diagnostic of this enriched gas. In massive halos, O VI column densities are strongly coupled to supermassive black hole growth, making the ion a sensitive indicator of AGN-driven metal redistribution. While many cosmological simulations have historically underpredicted O VI column densities compared to the COS-Halos survey, models incorporating robust supermassive black hole feedback have recently succeeded in reproducing these observations, such as the ROMULUS25 simulation [Sanchez et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...882....8S/abstract).

The kinematics of O VI further underscore the complexity of the CGM. While absorption features frequently trace virialized halo gas and bipolar outflows [Ng et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...886...66N/abstract), recent simulations predict that O VI emission primarily originates from clumpy, collisionally ionized ($T \sim 10^{5.5}$ K) inflowing recycled gas in galactic fountains rather than direct outflows [Lochhaas et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251025844L/abstract). In the dwarf regime, this warm gas phase ($10^{4.5} - 10^{5.5}$ K) dominates the CGM mass beyond half the virial radius, retaining $5-10\%$ of the metals formed by the galaxy despite high overall mass loss fractions [Piacitelli et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250508861P/abstract).

## Dynamics of the Baryon Cycle: Inflows, Outflows, and Recycling

The circumgalactic medium (CGM) is not merely a static reservoir of diffuse gas, but rather a dynamic ecosystem that acts as the primary engine of galaxy evolution [Tumlinson et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ARA&A..55..389T/abstract). The dynamics of the baryon cycle are governed by a continuous competition between [[galactic-outflows-and-inflows|Galactic Outflows and Inflows]], the condensation of fresh accreting gas, and the recycling of metal-enriched material.

**Inflows and Condensation**
Gas accretion from the CGM onto the interstellar medium (ISM) is the primary driver of star formation, but it is strongly sensitive to the thermodynamic stability of the halo. Empirical estimates using H$\alpha$ emission demonstrate that CGM mass cooling rates can exceed galactic star formation rates by factors of 4 to 90. This severe imbalance physically necessitates vigorous feedback to prevent the catastrophic over-collection of cold gas within the ISM [Zhang et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...916..101Z/abstract). To accurately constrain these mass flows, recent analytical frameworks have provided improved methodologies for converting empirical absorption spectrum measurements into global estimates of condensed matter mass densities across the multi-scale, multi-phase CGM [Peroux et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241107988P/abstract). Furthermore, the broader environment plays a critical role in these dynamics; observations of the Virgo Cluster demonstrate that dense cluster environments can severely suppress and truncate the CGM, potentially quenching star formation entirely via gas starvation [Yoon et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...772L..29Y/abstract).

**Gas Recycling and Galactic Fountains**
A significant fraction of the mass ejected by stellar and AGN feedback does not permanently escape the dark matter halo. Instead, it forms [[galactic-fountains|Galactic fountains]] that eventually re-accrete. The angular momentum of the host galaxy strongly influences this recycling topology: high-angular momentum galaxies exhibit biconical polar outflows and large wedges of rotating cold gas extending into the CGM [DeFelippis et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020ApJ...895...17D/abstract). This topology is evident in systems with centrally concentrated star formation, such as 'breakBRD' galaxies. These systems exhibit low CGM angular momentum coupled with high CGM metallicity, a signature indicating that their baryon cycles are dominated by recycling rather than fresh cosmological accretion from the intergalactic medium [Tonnesen et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...951...16T/abstract). The material participating in these fountains is heavily metal-enriched. For example, highly ionized oxygen (O VI) emission in the CGM often traces clumpy, inflowing recycled gas rather than pristine accretion or purely outflowing material, underscoring the importance of galactic fountains in mixing metals into the accreting gas supply [Lochhaas et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251025844L/abstract). 

**Cosmic Evolution of Net Flows**
The balance between these competing mass transfer rates shifts over cosmic time. Cosmological simulations such as IllustrisTNG reveal that at high redshifts ($z \gtrsim 2$), galaxies experience strong [[net-gas-inflows|Net gas inflows]] on both halo and ISM scales, fueling rapid mass assembly. At later epochs, outflows and inflows nearly balance, aided by the onset of kinetic AGN feedback in massive halos [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract). Furthermore, these models indicate that while [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy loading]] remains relatively constant across mass and redshift, mass loading steadily decreases as halo mass and redshift increase, reflecting the evolving efficiency of the global baryon cycle [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract).

## Self-Regulation and the Precipitation Limit

The circumgalactic medium (CGM) serves as the primary arena for [[self-regulated-feedback-mechanisms|Self-regulated feedback mechanisms]], where the balance between radiative cooling and energetic feedback dictates the growth of galaxies. A prevailing theoretical framework posits that feedback maintains the CGM in a state of marginal thermal stability, commonly referred to as the precipitation limit [Voit et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...808L..30V/abstract). This emergent equilibrium state is characterized by the dimensionless ratio of the local cooling time to the gravitational freefall time, $t_{\rm cool}/t_{\rm ff}$.

When the CGM pressure rises or cooling accelerates such that $t_{\rm cool}/t_{\rm ff} \lesssim 10$, the hot atmosphere becomes susceptible to multiphase thermal instabilities. Cold gas clouds condense and "rain" down toward the central galaxy, fueling star formation and accretion onto supermassive black holes. The ensuing feedback rapidly injects energy into the surrounding gas, reheating the CGM, causing the atmosphere to expand, and restoring the ratio to $t_{\rm cool}/t_{\rm ff} \gtrsim 10$ [Voit et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019arXiv190311212V/abstract), [Voit et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...908L..16V/abstract). 

Within this framework, the parameters governing outflow efficiency—namely the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] ($\eta_M$) and [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy loading factor]] ($\eta_E$)—dictate a galaxy's [[equilibrium-star-formation-rates|Equilibrium star formation rates]]. The classical assumption that a higher mass loading factor invariably suppresses galaxy growth has been challenged by recent atmospheric equilibrium models. In low-mass galaxies, increasing $\eta_M$ can counterintuitively result in *more* star formation. When large amounts of mass are ejected into the lower halo, more supernova energy is continually required to resist atmospheric contraction, forcing the system to settle at a higher equilibrium star formation rate [Voit et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240607631V/abstract).

Despite the explanatory power of the precipitation limit, the literature remains divided on the exact physical trigger for large-scale regulation. While many studies assert that galaxy growth is explicitly bottlenecked by the $t_{\rm cool}/t_{\rm ff} \approx 10$ threshold, other structural models argue that self-regulation emerges from a direct balance of momentum and energy injection against the galactic gravitational potential, functioning independently of any specific cooling-time ratio [Hopkins et al. (2011)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011MNRAS.417..950H/abstract), [Katz et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241107282K/abstract).

## Numerical Implementation and Subgrid Physics

Because cosmological simulations cannot resolve the parsec-scale physical processes of individual supernovae or supermassive black hole accretion, energy and momentum injection must be modeled using subgrid recipes. Early numerical implementations that simply injected thermal energy into the surrounding gas suffered from the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]]. Because star formation occurs in dense, rapidly cooling regions, the injected thermal energy radiated away before it could do the mechanical work required to drive galactic winds. To circumvent this, early models relied on ad-hoc numerical workarounds, such as temporarily disabling radiative cooling or imposing explicit outward kinetic kicks on gas particles. 

Modern simulations have shifted toward more physically motivated implementations that account for early, pre-supernova feedback. Subgrid recipes now frequently incorporate [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] and [[radiation-pressure|Radiation pressure]], which clear dense gas within the first $\sim 3$ Myr of a giant molecular cloud's life [Chevance et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509..272C/abstract), [Lucas et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020MNRAS.493.4700L/abstract). By reducing the local ambient density, this early feedback minimizes radiative losses, allowing subsequent supernova energy to effectively escape the interstellar medium (ISM) and heat the circumgalactic medium (CGM) [Agertz et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...770...25A/abstract). To accurately capture the localized physics of these outflows—such as the expansion of hot gas bubbles and the venting of chimneys—simulations must achieve spatial resolutions better than 50 pc to avoid over-relying on sub-resolution prescriptions [Ceverino et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008IAUS..245...33C/abstract). Studies comparing thermal, kinetic, and [[mechanical-feedback|Mechanical feedback]] models show that while global star formation rates may appear similar across different recipes, the resulting thermodynamic structure of the ISM varies drastically [Agertz et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013ApJ...770...25A/abstract). Currently, mechanical feedback implementations provide the most robust match to observed mass-metallicity relations up to redshift $z \sim 3$ [Ibrahim et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024MNRAS.527.3276I/abstract), [Ibrahim et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.544..815I/abstract). Modern codes also grapple with the challenges of incorporating detailed dust physics, such as dust grain formation, growth, and destruction, which are vital for tracking the true multi-phase thermodynamic state of the ISM and CGM [Parente et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250410585P/abstract). To bridge the gap between complex theoretical structures and empirical data, researchers increasingly rely on idealized spatial-kinematic absorption models (SKAMs). Rather than post-processing hydrodynamical simulation outputs, SKAMs serve as standalone mathematical frameworks that synthesize realistic multiphase absorption line profiles from parameterized structural components (such as disks, halos, and winds) to explore theoretical scenarios of the baryon cycle [Churchill et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023803C/abstract).

The choice of subgrid physics directly dictates the balance of the [[mass-loading-factor|Mass loading factor]] ($\eta_M$) and [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy-loading factor]] ($\eta_E$). In the IllustrisTNG suite, for example, the subgrid wind model yields a mass loading that decreases with both increasing halo mass and increasing redshift, whereas the energy loading remains nearly constant [Oren et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251023343O/abstract). The specific modeling approaches can produce uniquely distinct evolutionary outcomes; the TNG50-1 simulation reveals striking dynamical similarities between ultra-diffuse galaxies and standard dwarf galaxies, suggesting they share a common dynamical lineage shaped by internal feedback loops [Nandi et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250622074N/abstract). However, comparisons between different simulation suites reveal significant tensions in the literature regarding the "correct" subgrid approach. Analysis of the CAMELS project—which varies subgrid parameters across the IllustrisTNG, SIMBA, and Astrid frameworks—demonstrates that these models produce wildly different CGM gas fractions and baryon distributions despite matching empirical stellar mass relations [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...967...32M/abstract), [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241016361M/abstract). SIMBA’s aggressive implementation of [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] couples more efficiently to the baryons, driving them further into the halo and resulting in a smoother distribution with lower variance in fast radio burst (FRB) dispersion measures [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...967...32M/abstract). In the realm of AGN feedback modeling, Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) cosmological simulations frequently implement dual jet and heating mechanisms to robustly regulate black hole growth and systematically drive these large-scale outflows [Dubois et al. (2012)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2012ASPC..453..281D/abstract). To accurately model the broader cosmic web, simulations also employ derived master equations that capture the evolving temperature and ionization state of composite, inhomogeneous intergalactic medium (IGM) phases while rigorously accounting for inflows and outflows [Manrique et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015ApJ...803..103M/abstract). Interestingly, the topological signatures of these feedback mechanisms, when analyzed via Minkowski functionals, are shown to persist on massive scales of up to tens of megaparsecs [Schimd et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240604430S/abstract).

Furthermore, subgrid implementations highlight the complex, non-linear coupling between stellar winds and AGN feedback. Traditional analytical models often treat these as independent processes, but numerical studies reveal they can mutually weaken one another. For instance, strong stellar feedback lowers central gas densities, which can delay the onset of AGN feedback and shift its peak efficiency to higher halo masses [Booth et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013NatSR...3.1738B/abstract), [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241016361M/abstract). The precise resolution and treatment of these [[galactic-gas-dynamics-and-flows|gas dynamics]] remains a central challenge in modeling [[multi-scale-multi-science-systems|multi-scale]] cosmic ecosystems.

## Observational Constraints and Multi-wavelength Mapping

Constraining the delicate balance between mass and energy loading requires empirical probes of the multiphase circumgalactic medium (CGM), which acts as the primary reservoir for a galaxy's recycled baryons and metals [Tumlinson et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2017ARA&A..55..389T/abstract). By tracing gas spanning orders of magnitude in temperature and density, multi-wavelength observations assess the kinematic and thermodynamic signatures of feedback. Locally, the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) serves as a primary laboratory for such multi-wavelength studies, offering an unprecedented, resolved view of the multi-phase feedback from [[massive-star-physics|massive young stellar objects]] (YSOs) and mature stars [Chu et al. (2010)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2011BSRSL..80..297C/abstract).

**Quasar Absorption Lines and UV Spectroscopy**
Ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy of background quasars remains the workhorse for probing cool ($T \sim 10^4$ K) and warm ($T \sim 10^{5.5}$ K) CGM phases. High-ionization states like O VI are highly sensitive to the energy injected by [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]], yet hydrodynamical simulations have historically struggled to reproduce the large O VI column densities observed by the COS-Halos survey, highlighting uncertainties in heavy element mixing and energy coupling [Sanchez et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...882....8S/abstract). Furthermore, current observational efforts are directly linking dynamically measured black hole masses to the column densities and kinematics of highly ionized gas in the CGM, probing the exact energy yields of AGN activity [Werk et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021hst..prop16650W/abstract). The kinematics of O VI absorbers exhibit a strong halo mass dependence, with velocity dispersions maximizing in $L^*$ galaxies where virial temperatures align with the collisionally ionized O VI fraction [Ng et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...886...66N/abstract). Recent large-scale surveys of low-ionization transitions, such as Mg II, reveal that cool gas covering fractions increase with redshift and strongly anti-correlate with stellar mass at small impact parameters ($< 0.3 R_{\rm vir}$) [Chang et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251203845C/abstract). In star-forming galaxies, this Mg II absorption is found to be strongest along the minor axis, providing clear evidence that star-formation-driven outflows are responsible for enhancing the cool gas content of the CGM in these polar directions [Chen et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJ...981...81C/abstract). Furthermore, observations from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) of emission-line galaxies at $z \sim 1.5$ reveal distinct kinematics between cool (Mg II) and warm (C IV) gas phases, highlighting the complex velocity structures of the multi-phase CGM at cosmic noon [Lan et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251103195L/abstract). Beyond individual sightlines, rest-frame UV spectroscopy remains critically important for tracing low-density gas dispersed by starburst-driven winds and analyzing their widespread interactions with the intergalactic medium [Martin et al. (1998)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1999ASPC..164...66M/abstract). 

**The Sunyaev-Zeldovich Effect and Fast Radio Bursts**
To constrain the hot and highly ionized components on halo scales, the thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect and Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) provide critical aggregate measurements. The thermal SZ signal traces the integrated electron pressure profile of the CGM. However, forward-modeling these signals reveals significant tensions: modern simulation suites (e.g., CAMELS) often fail to reproduce the SZ profiles observed around massive galaxy samples, pointing to inaccuracies in modeled feedback energies [Moser et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...933..133M/abstract). Furthermore, the inference of CGM properties from SZ data is highly sensitive to modeling choices, such as the treatment of the two-halo term [Moser et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021ApJ...919....2M/abstract). Concurrently, the dispersion measures (DMs) of FRBs offer a direct census of ionized column densities. Recent local FRB localizations constrain the Milky Way's total CGM mass to $< 10^{11} M_\odot$ [Ravi et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025AJ....169..330R/abstract). To better isolate the CGM's contribution in these FRB data, researchers have developed high-fidelity dispersion measure models for the local universe ($D < 120$ Mpc) that carefully map the cosmic web's electron density [Huang et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241022098H/abstract). Alongside FRBs, traditional radio emission remains vital for identifying feedback mechanisms, tracing the shocked ISM caused by various AGN-driven outflow modes [Harrison et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024Galax..12...17H/abstract). On cosmic scales, the variance in FRB DMs is proving to be heavily dependent on the assumed subgrid efficiency of [[galactic-outflows-and-feedback|Galactic Outflows and Feedback]], with AGN rather than supernovae dominating the large-scale redistribution of baryons [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...967...32M/abstract).

**Line Emission Mapping and Future Missions**
Looking toward higher redshifts and diffuse gas, upcoming line intensity mapping provides a novel statistical probe. Predictions using the CoDa III simulation indicate that H$\alpha$ line intensity mapping will be a powerful tool for tracing the intergalactic medium and broad galaxy feedback effects during the Epoch of Reionization [Lee et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025RNAAS...9...96L/abstract). Direct imaging of the hot ($T > 10^6$ K) CGM also represents a crucial frontier for measuring the mechanical energy of feedback. Currently, diffuse soft X-ray emission around local $L^*$ galaxies has been detected out to $\sim 50$ kpc via stacking analyses with eROSITA [He et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260116499H/abstract). However, mock observations demonstrate that different subgrid models (e.g., SIMBA vs. EAGLE) produce widely varying surface brightness profiles, driven by density differences at small radii and temperature variations further out [Grayson et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250609123G/abstract). Overcoming these ambiguities requires future high-resolution observatories. Next-generation sensitive X-ray telescopes have the potential to revolutionize individual detections of this hot CGM component around normal galaxies [Oppenheimer et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019BAAS...51c.280O/abstract). Proposed missions such as the Line Emission Mapper (LEM) and the Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS) will map soft X-ray line emission with $1-2$ eV spectral resolution [Kraft et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022arXiv221109827K/abstract), [Russell et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024Univ...10..273R/abstract). Complementary to X-ray observatories, the proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) presents a compelling science case for mapping faint CGM emission lines in the ultraviolet and optical, which will allow for the detailed investigation of small-scale thermal instabilities and galactic winds [Burchett et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250703750B/abstract). By resolving individual emission lines, these future observatories will definitively close the mass and energy budgets of galaxy halos.

## Open Questions and Future Directions

Despite advances in theoretical modeling and observational diagnostics, the exact mechanics of baryon cycling through the circumgalactic medium (CGM) remain highly contested. A central challenge in contemporary astrophysics is reconciling the varying theoretical implementations of feedback with direct multi-wavelength observations across cosmic time.

A prominent unresolved issue is the "missing baryons problem" in Milky Way-mass halos. Recent measurements of dispersion measures from Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) constrain the mass of the Milky Way's CGM to $< 10^{11}\ M_\odot$, suggesting that the total baryonic mass of the Galaxy is $\lesssim 60\%$ of the cosmological average for its halo mass [Ravi et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025AJ....169..330R/abstract). This implies that massive quantities of baryons have been expelled beyond the virial radius. However, simulations struggle to consistently reproduce the thermodynamic state of this extended gas; for instance, while some modern models have succeeded, many historical cosmological models frequently underproduce the column densities of O VI observed by the COS-Halos survey [Sanchez et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019ApJ...882....8S/abstract), and varying models predict vastly different Sunyaev-Zeldovich pressure profiles [Moser et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...933..133M/abstract).

These discrepancies stem directly from uncertainties in the exact coupling efficiency of energy and momentum to the multi-phase ISM. Because the coupling efficiency of [[stellar-feedback-and-winds|Stellar Feedback and Winds]] and [[active-galactic-nuclei-agn-physics|Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) Physics]] cannot be resolved from first principles in cosmological volumes, different subgrid implementations yield wildly divergent CGM gas fractions and metal distributions, even when they successfully reproduce the same $z=0$ stellar mass relations [Medlock et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...967...32M/abstract), [Grayson et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250609123G/abstract). The literature is also conflicted on the non-linear interaction of multiple feedback modes. While standard semi-analytic models often treat supernova and AGN feedback as independent or additive, hydrodynamical simulations indicate they can mutually weaken each other by up to an order of magnitude in the halo mass range for which both feedback processes are efficient [Booth et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013NatSR...3.1738B/abstract).

The theoretical framework governing macroscopic regulation is similarly debated. While standard models solve the [[overcooling-problem|Overcooling problem]] via purely ejective feedback (high mass-loading), emerging theories suggest that self-regulation may be fundamentally [[negative-feedback|preventative]], relying heavily on [[galactic-outflows-and-wind-energetics|energy-loading]] to balance the CGM's thermodynamic state. In this paradigm, Milky Way-mass halos prefer $\eta_E \sim 0.1$ with low $\eta_M$ [Carr et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023ApJ...949...21C/abstract). 

Finally, the applicability of locally calibrated feedback models to high-redshift galaxies remains highly uncertain [Katz et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241107282K/abstract). The advent of JWST has revealed unique conditions in the early universe, including unexplained $z > 5$ nitrogen excesses that may be excited by $75-150\text{ km s}^{-1}$ radiative shocks driven by early winds [Flury et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv241206763F/abstract). High-redshift galaxies appear highly efficient at baryon removal, exhibiting empirical mass loading factors ranging from $\eta_M \approx 0.04$ to $0.4$ [Saldana-Lopez et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250117145S/abstract). Furthermore, there is growing evidence that energetic feedback in the early universe ($z \gtrsim 6$) frequently operated as [[positive-feedback-astrophysics|Positive feedback (astrophysics)]], triggering rather than suppressing star formation via pressure compression, before transitioning to the quenching, energy-conserving outflows observed at lower redshifts [Silk et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024ApJ...961L..39S/abstract). Resolving these tensions and tracking the full flow of metals through cosmic ecosystems will ultimately require the next generation of high-resolution spectrographs alongside advanced X-ray observatories [Lehner et al. (2019)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019BAAS...51c.473L/abstract), [Saracco et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv251217042S/abstract).
